courses.description: This course will provide an overview of various topics in food science and technology. Lectures will include discussions of general areas of interest chosen to stimulate and foster students' interest in both food science and food technology. The course will cover topics that include basic food chemistry, food processing and preservation, food microbiology and fermentation, food safety and toxicology, food engineering, food biotechnology, food evaluation and product development, etc. Relevant examples will be cited to strengthen the basic understanding of the principles in each topic. Local issues related to food will also be discussed.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Define Food Science and Food Technology
- Understand the dimensions of food processing and preservation
- Grasp the basic information in food chemistry, food microbiology and food product development, and be able to utilize them in the preparation of safe and high quality food products
- Tell the current trends and advancements in Food Science and Technology

courses.description: This course provides an overview of the basic concepts and principles of nutrition science and how to apply the principles of good nutrition in everyday life to the planning of healthy eating for optimal health, performance and disease prevention. Students will also be able to identify some common Hong Kong nutrition problems and the role of nutrition in their origins, prevention and therapy. The course will also expose the students to some additional nutritional issues of current health or research significance.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Define the science of nutrition, and discuss the importance of nutritional adequacy and balance for optimal growth and health
- Identify the dietary sources, functions and key roles in health protection of the major nutrients

courses.description:
Ethics are principles that governing a person’s professional behaviour. Students need to understand what is and what is not professional behaviour. Therefore, this course will cover the issues of professional behavior, including Association for Nutrition (AfN) Standards for Ethics, Conduct and Performance. Other topics relating to professionalism, such as intellectual property issues, preventing from corruption behavior, handling of privacy/personal data, etc. will also be covered in this course.

To apply for the Nutritionist stream (FNS-NS), students must pass the course with at least a C in this course along with other FNS-NS admission requirements.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. analyze what is and what is not professional behaviour,
2. remember and understand the standards of ethics, conduct and performance set by AfN,
3. describe intellectual property issues, how to avoid corruption, and property ways of handling privacy data

3. demonstrate a good knowledge in the official methods of food chemical analyses
4. understand the principles and operations of modern analytical instruments such as GC-MS and HPLC for the food
composition analyses
5. use various methods to enumerate the number of microorganisms in foods and determine if a product meets the
microbial levels listed in specifications, guidelines, or standard
6. understand the selective activity of growth media and identify specific microorganisms important to food importance
7. apply the appropriate concepts and analytical methods when presented with a practical problem
8. demonstrate practical proficiency in a food testing and analysis laboratory

courses.description: Since our body is experiencing changes in the life cycle, the nutrition needs would be different in various stages. This course describes the basis of these needs. Furthermore, the assessment of nutrient intake and physiology of our body in different life-cycle stages will be discussed. Prevention of chronic diseases through prudent dietary practices will also be introduced.
courses.learning_outcomes:
FNSC3010 contains eight parts:
Part I: Introduction to the role of nutrition in the life cycle
Part II: Maternal Nutrition
Part III: Lactation and Human Milk
Part IV: Nutrition during Infancy
Part V: Nutrition in Childhood
Part VI: Nutrition in Adolescence
Part VII: Nutrition during Adulthood
Part VIII: Nutrition for the Elderly

The learning outcomes:
PART I Introduction to the role of nutrition in the life cycle
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Define a nutrient and an essential nutrient and list the six classes of nutrients found in foods.
• Define the dietary reference intakes (DRI) and state who develops the DRI.
• Discuss to whom the DRI apply and how DRI are used.
• Define the four categories of DRI namely Estimated Average Requirement (EAR), Recommended Dietary
• Allowance (RDA), Adequate Intake (AI) and Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL).
• Describe the judgment factors involved in setting the energy and nutrient intake.
• Identify the functions of brown fat tissue in energy metabolism.
• List methods used in nutrition surveys and describe the kinds of information these surveys can provide.
• Describe advantages and disadvantages of each method used in nutrition survey?
• Define the malnutrition, undernutrition and overnutrition.
• List the diet-planning principles and describe how each principle helps in diet planning.
• Describe the major food groups and their nutrient profile and how to use food groups in planning a diet.
• Describe how food pyramid (old or new) is developed and its limitations.
• List the information you can expect to find on a food label.
• Define the Daily Values and describe how they can help you meet health recommendation.

PART II Maternal Nutrition
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Describe the physiological changes in pregnancy.
• Identify the mechanisms by which the plasma glucose level is regulated differently in pregnant women.
• Explain the metabolic changes in macronutrients and the special needs for various nutrients.
• Identify the behavioral as well as environmental conditions that may jeopardize the pregnancy.
• Describe the influences of maternal dietary intake on the fetus.
• Identify the health effect on the mother and the fetus for teenage pregnancy.
• Assess the nutrition status during pregnancy.

PART III Lactation and Human Milk
Objective: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Describe the physiology of lactation
• Describe how RDAs are established for lactating women.
• Explain how maternal nutrients and immune factors are transported to the milk.
• Describe the features of human milk and the advantages over formulas.
• Identify substances consumed by the mother inducing health problems to the infant.
• Diagnose failure-to-thrive for breastfed infants.

PART IV Nutrition during Infancy
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Identify the major dietary factors influencing growth and maturation.
• Use of Growth Chart for assessing nutrition and health condition in infancy.
• Describe the development of digestion and absorption in early infancy.
• Describe the nutrient needs during infancy.
• Assess the nutrition status during infancy.

PART V Nutrition in Childhood
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Explain the nutrient needs for children at preschool and school age.
• Discuss factors that affect food choice.
• Assess the nutrition status during childhood.
• Explain the possibility of chronic disease initiation arisen from childhood nutrition.
• Identify the health effect of vegetarian diet on childhood.

PART VI Nutrition in Adolescence
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Assess the nutrition status in adolescence.
• Describe the growth and development and the nutrient needs.
• Describe rapid growth in adolescence and how it relates to an orderly process of sexual maturation.
• Describe the body composition changes associated with adolescent growth and differences between male and
female.
• Describe the specific nutrient requirement for adolescents to support their growth.
• Describe the common nutritional disorders that adolescents are likely to have.
• Describe how diet of the adolescents affects growth and physical performance and may influence behavior and
future risk of chronic diseases.
• Describe the change in nutrient needs from childhood to adolescence.
• Describe why an adolescent girl is more likely to develop an iron deficiency than is a boy.
• Describe the criterion to assess the anemia.
• Describe why iron, zinc and calcium are so important for adolescents.
• Describe the problems associated with childhood/adolescent obesity and the strategies for prevention and
treatment.
• Discuss the major factors in contribution to childhood/adolescent obesity.
• Describe eating disorders, Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimic Nervosa, and the possible factors for these eating
disorders.

PART VII Nutrition during Adulthood
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Describe various dietary recommendations for population at risk of chronic diseases.
• Describe dietary recommendation for general health.
• Explain potential health problems caused by unhealthy diets.
• Plan for a healthy lifestyle on the top of prudent dietary habits.
• Describe the major factors in contribution to the heart diseases
• Describe the major dietary factors that affect cancer development
• Describe the major factors leading to hypertension.

PART VIII Nutrition in the Elderly
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• Describe the physiological changes of ageing.
• Describe the major theories of ageing.
• Describe the anti-ageing theory of antioxidant and free radicals.
• Describe the osteoporosis and concern in calcium deficiency.
• Define the nutrient requirements for the elderly.
• Explain the food selection of the elderly.

•描述人乳的特点和相比的优势公式。

•描述婴儿期消化和吸收的发展。
•描述在婴儿期的营养需要。
•评估婴儿期的营养状况。

第五部分 儿童营养
目标：经过这些讲座，学生应该能够

•讨论食物选择的影响因素。
•评估在儿童时期的营养状况。
•解释儿童营养导致慢性疾病的可能性，。

第六部分 青少年营养

meetings.instructor: Professor CHOW Hei Man

courses.description: This component will provide students with the background required to appreciate the biochemical aspects of nutrition and the impact of nutrition-related factors on normal human biochemistry. Areas covered include the digestion and absorption of nutrients, energy intake and expenditure, nutrition and metabolism of carbohydrate, cholesterol synthesis and homeostasis, metabolism of dietary fats and their effect on lipoprotein cholesterol, nitrogen metabolism, and minerals and vitamins and their roles in biochemical processes.
courses.learning_outcomes:
FNSC3030 contains six parts:
PART I Energy and metabolism, intake and expenditure
PART II Nutrition and metabolism of carbohydrates
PART III Nutrition and metabolism of proteins
PART IV Nutrition and metabolism of vitamins
PART V Nutrition and metabolism of fats
PART VI Metabolism of cholesterol and lipoproteins

The learning outcomes:
PART I Energy intake, expenditure and metabolism
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• describe changes in body composition from birth to adulthood.
• define the basal metabolic rate (BMR), resting metabolic rate (RMR), and diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT).
• describe the methods used in estimating BMR and RMR.
• calculate the energy content of a mixed diet
• identify the functions of brown fat tissue in energy metabolism.
• describe the role of carbohydrate in energy metabolism.

PART II Nutrition and metabolism of carbohydrates
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• identify the mechanisms by which the plasma glucose level is regulated.
• define the glycemic index and explain how it is useful in the control of diabetes mellitus.
• outline the metabolic differences between glucose and fructose.
• describe the influences of dietary fructose on plasma LDL-cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol and triglyceride and explain the possible mechanisms involved.
• define insoluble and soluble fibers, and give some examples and source of each.
• identify the health effect of dietary fibers and explain the possible mechanisms involved.
• explain the biochemical basis of major inborn disorders of carbohydrate metabolism.
• list some major commercial artificial sweeteners and some specific characteristics of each.

PART III Nutrition and metabolism of proteins
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• define the essential amino acids.
• define nitrogen balance and its application in the determination of protein requirement.
• identify the general steps by which amino acids are converted to glucose in fasting and starvation.
• explain the biochemical basis of homocystinuria and its atherogenic effect.
• explain the biochemical basis of phenylketonuria.
• describe the differences between animal and plant proteins.
• identify the positive and negative effects of vegetarian diets.

PART IV Nutrition and metabolism of vitamins
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• describe the functions of fat-soluble vitamins.
• describe the structures and functions of B vitamins.
• define the term coenzymes and their role in energy metabolism.
• explain why some vitamins are essential to energy metabolism.
• describe some common biochemical tests to assess the vitamin status.
• describe the symptoms of various vitamin deficiency diseases.

PART V Nutrition and metabolism of fats
Objective: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• describe the nomenclature of lipids used in nutrition.
• describe the characteristics of omega-3, omega-6 and omega-9 fatty acids.
• identify the characteristic features of vegetable oils, fish oil and animal fats, and their potential nutritional significance.
• identify the biochemical pathway by which linoleic acid is converted to arachidonic acid.
• identify the biochemical pathway by which -linolenic acid is converted to docosahexaenoic acid.
• identify the biochemical pathway by which oleic acid is converted to eicosatrienoic acid.
• list the chemical reactions and enzymes involved in chain-elongation and -desuration.
• identify the enzymes and biochemical pathway in fatty acid synthesis.
• understand the mechanisms by which dietary fatty acid composition affects lipogenesis.
• describe the possible health effects of trans fatty acids.
• list some common fat substitutes and the proposed use in food industry.
• explain why olestra is neither digested nor absorbed.

PART VI Nutrition and metabolism of cholesterol and lipoproteins
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
• identify the major dietary factors influencing the level of plasma cholesterol.
• identify the biochemical pathway by which cholesterol is synthesized and degraded.
• describe the roles of cholesterol-7-hydroxylase and acyl CoA: cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT) in metabolism of cholesterol.
• classify the inborn lipoprotein disorders.
• describe the processes by which cholesterol is digested, mobilized and transported in the body.
• define the hyperlipoproteinemia.
• understand the mechanism by which dietary plant sterols decrease the risk of atherosclerosis.

courses.description: This course will cover the basic chemical and analytical aspects of major food components (water, carbohydrates, lipids and proteins) and minor food components (vitamins, minerals, pigments and food additives including flavors, colorants and preservatives). Emphasis will be made on the chemical reactions and changes in these food constituents during processing, handling and storage. The principles and applications of chemical and instrumental analysis of food will be illustrated. The actions and applications of enzymes in food manufacture and food spoilage will be discussed.
courses.learning_outcomes:
This course contributes as one of the core competencies in food science.
After the students have finished the learning activities in FNSC3110, they will be able to:
 Understand the chemistry underlying the properties and reactions of various food components
 Have sufficient knowledge of food chemistry to control reactions in foods
 Understand the major chemical reactions that limit shelf life of foods
 Understand the principles behind analytical techniques associated with food
The detailed content of the course is as follows:
Teaching: 37 lecture hours and mid-term examination: 2 lecture hours
I. Water [2 lectures]
 Water structure: physical characteristics and water-solute interactions
 Water activity: definition, sorption isotherms
 Reaction rates and water content: physical changes, chemical reactions and microbial growth
 Importance of water activity
II. Food Carbohydrates [6 lectures]
Classification of food carbohydrates
Chromatographic analysis of carbohydrates
Food-related chemical reactions of carbohydrates
Functional properties of food polysaccharides
Dietary fiber: definition, constituents and methods of analysis
III. Food Lipids [5 lectures]
 Fatty acids: nomenclature and saturation
 Analysis of lipids
 Chemical degradation: rancidity (oxidation) and effects of heat
 Physical properties of triglycerides
 Emulsions and emulsifiers
 Fat replacers and mimetics
 Fats and oils in the marketplace
 Hydrogenation and Trans fatty acids
IV. Food Proteins [5 lectures]
 Protein classification and structure
 Protein denaturation
 Chemical changes in proteins
 Functional properties of proteins
 Food proteins from animal and plant origins
V. Food Additives and Contaminants [5 lectures]
Food additives: purposes, definitions and functional categories
Local issues on food additives
Selected examples of food additives: their properties and applications
Contaminants (incidental additives)
VI. Food Colorants [4 lectures]
 Natural food pigments
Tetrapyrrole pigments - myoglobin and chlorophyll
Isoprenoid derivatives - carotenoids
Benzopyran derivatives – anthocyanins and flavonoids
 Artificial/synthetic colorants
Certified color dyes and lakes
Regulatory and safety aspects
VII. Micronutrients [5 lectures]
Vitamins: sources, degradation and functional properties
Fat-soluble (Vitamin A and E)
Water-soluble (C and B1)
Chemical analysis
Vitamins: colorimetric and HPLC methods
Mineral: ashing procedures and atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS)
VIII. Food Enzymes [5 lectures]
 Classification and numbering system
 General applications of food enzymes
 Specific examples of food enzymes
Hydrolysis of starch by amylases
Pectic enzymes and fruit juice processing
Proteases in milk and cheese production
Polyphenol oxidases and enzymatic browning
Lipases and lipoxygenases for flavor and off-flavors development

courses.description: This course considers the microorganisms in food safety, spoilage, and production. • To obtain an integrated picture of food microbiology
• To learn to address the problems as a food microbiologist
• To learn to address the"how" and "why" and "what can we do about it" questions regarding the activities of microbes in food.
• To understand that there is no simple answers to these questions or simple solutions to the problems we are studying
• To learn to make the best decisions among the many alternatives and to designing the most creative new approaches.
• To learn to analyse a situation, e.g. a food poisoning outbreak, hypothesize what would have happened to cause the situation and suggest an improvement.

Part I: Introduction
Introduction to Food Microbiology
What food microbiology should include the following of food-borne microbes:
Ecology
Physiology
Epidemiology
Pathology

The basic biology of various microorganisms--fungi, bacteria, viruses

To know the action of toxins on the gasterointestinal cells

To learn the biology, ecology, pathology, disease pictures, transmission paths, and control measures of S. aureus
Emerging Bacterial Pathogens
To understand the factors leading to the emergence of some bacteria as food-borne pathogens
To learn the biology, ecology, pathology, disease pictures, transmission paths, and control measures of the emerging bacterial pathogens including:

Escherichia coli O157:H7

To learn the biology, ecology, pathology, disease pictures, transmission paths, and control measures of the food-borne viruses

To learn the biology, ecology, pathology, disease pictures, transmission paths, and control measures of Protozoa and Parasitic Worms
Fungal Toxins in Food
To understand the kind of fungal toxins in foods and their actions

Application of investigation results
Essential steps for investigation of food-borne disease outbreaks
The things to look for in an investigation
To know how to investigate food-borne disease outbreaks

To learn the effects of the environmental parameters on growth and survival of microorganisms
Temperature Effects on Microbial Growth and Survival
Thermal Destruction Kinetics and Calculations
Water Activity as a Parameter of Survival and Growth
Acids as Food Preservatives
Effect of Atmosphere on Microbial Growth and Survival
To acquire the ability to analyze food for spoilage possibilities
To learn Microbial Food Spoilage Patterns
To understand Controversial Preservation Methods: Nitrite, Antibiotics, and Food Irradiation

Part V: Microbial and fermented foods
To understand why we make fermented foods
To understand various kinds of food fermentations
Lactic Acid Bacteria and Lactic Fermentations
Fermentations Involving Extracellular Hydrolases And Other Complex Fermentations

Special topics:

1. The roles of HK SAR Government agencies to food safety and food hygiene in HK SAR I: Health, Wealth and Food Bureau

3. The roles of HK SAR Government agencies in HK SAR III: “Health Department”, “Agriculture, Fishery, and Conservation Department”, “Government Laboratory”, etc.
4. Food safety and public health in HK SAR : Import controls

8. Food safety in Food Supplies in HK SAR IV: Retails—markets and supermarkets

2. Critically analyze the information and data

5. Summarize the key observations and analyses
6. Suggest any improvement

courses.description: This is an integrated laboratory course for the food product production, which is composed of three interrelated areas, namely, food processing technology, food product development and food quality control. Through the food processing practicum, the principles, techniques and applications of conventional food processing technologies and equipment are introduced. Topics include frying, packaging, dehydration, concentration, sterilization, fermentation, protein coagulation, emulsification, baking, dough formation and candy making. This course also covers the techniques in formal sensory evaluation, and the principles of the common instruments for physical and chemical analyses of food quality. Besides, it contains an interactive workshop to explore the procedures in food product development in the contemporary catering and food industries.
courses.learning_outcomes:
This is a multidisciplinary laboratory course comprising of food processing practicum, sensory evaluation experiment, and the workshops on food hygiene and safety, food product development and quality control. After the students have finished these learning activities, they should be able to:
1. understand the principles of food processing technologies and their applications in different kinds of food production
2. understand the theories and recognize the critical techniques of various food unit operations
3. master the knowledge in the production process of daily food products
4. recognize the importance of good hygiene standard and safety measures in food production plant and laboratory
5. select and setup different sensory tests based on specific objectives, and use the statistical method for data analyses appropriately
6. identify the quality requirements for food products, and their corresponding examination procedures
7. comprehend the different stages involved in food product development, and apply the appropriate knowledge in the real situation

courses.description: In this course, students will examine the principles behind food processing technology, different kinds of conventional equipments and their effects on the sensory, microbiological and nutritional qualities of food e.g. meats, vegetable, fruits. Topics may also include food processing, waste management, etc., and basic principles of food engineering.
courses.learning_outcomes:
FNSC4110 contains four parts:
Part I: Introduction and basic principles
Part II: Ambient temperature processing
Part III: High temperature processing
Part IV: Low temperature processing

The learning outcomes:
Part I Introduction and basic principles
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Define and differentiate terminology such as food science, food technology, process, unit operation, etc.
 Describe what are process block diagram, process flow diagram, floor plan and 3-D process diagram
 Distinguish between phase and glass transition.
 Define density, bulk density and porosity
 Define absolute pressure, atmospheric pressure and gauge pressure
 Understand viscosity and its relationship with shear stress and shear rate in food, and related properties
 Calculate mass balance in a process and its function
 Understand the essence in the Bernoulli's equation in fluid flow
 Differentiate streamline and turbulent flow and application of the Reynolds number
 Differentiate among the conduction, convection and radiation.
 Understand the parameters involved in conduction and convection
 Able to make use the heat transfer coefficient, thermal conductivity and overall heat transfer coefficient in real life
application
 Differentiate between steady state and unsteady-state of heat transfer
 Define and apply biot number in specific conditions

Part II Ambient temperature processing
1. Raw material preparation
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand the features and requirements for raw material preparation
 Identify the types of common contaminants on raw foods and the methods of their detection and/or removal
 Compare the differences the principles and applications of dry and wet cleaning methods
 Understand the importance of sorting in food processing
 Classify the separation of raw materials into groups by their different physical properties including size, shape,
weight, density and color
 Examine the differences in the principles of equipments used for sorting
 Describe the factors used for grading
 Understand the methods of peeling and the considerations of choice

2. Size reduction
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand the importance of size reduction in food processing
 Correlate the nature of forces, physical properties and equipment design for size reduction in solid foods
 Explain homogenization and emulsification in liquid foods and their associated processing equipments
 Examine the effect of size reduction in solid and liquid foods in terms of sensory and nutritional values

3. Mixing
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand the objectives of mixing in food processing
 Describe the different mechanisms in solid mixing in relationship with the equipment design.
 Differentiate the different theories of liquid mixing based on viscosity in explaining the different designs of the
liquid mixers
 Understand the possible effect of mixing on foods

4. Mechanical separations
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Explain the principles of centrifugation in separating immiscible liquids or solids from liquids
 Examine the design and operations of centrifuges in different food applications
 Contrast the different means, of filtration (vacuum versus pressure) in association with the equipment, design and
operations
 Understand the use of compressive forces and other physical factors to produce oil and juice in batch, and
continuous modes of operations

5. Membrane concentration
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand this unit operation as pressure-activated using a semi-permeable membrane to separate
components in a solution or colloidal suspension
 Compare reverse osmosis and ultrafiltration in terms of theories and food applications
 Understand the advantages and limitations of membrane concentration over concentration by evaporation
 Describe the membrane materials and equipment design

6. Radiation
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be, able to
 Understand the advantages and limitations of irradiation
 Describe the theory and equipment used for food irradiation and its food applications
 Discuss the safety issues of food irradiation

Part III High temperature processing
1. Blanching
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Describe the purpose of blanching
 Differentiate the different enzymes which responsible for the quality deterioration
 Tell the function of indicator enzymes
 Describe the heating sources of blancher and their pros and cons of function
 Describe the criteria of idea equipment
 Name the different types of blanchers and their features
 Describe how they affect the quality of foods

2. Heat sterilization
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Describe the purpose of heat sterilization
 Define commercial sterilization
 Elaborate the 12D, 5D concept
 Differentiate two different, types of sterilization
 Describe the factors affecting sterilization time and how it is determined
 Read "D" and "z" and their implications
 Describe how the pH or acidity affects the heat resistance of microorganism and enzymes
 Describe the importance of monitoring the rate of heat penetration and factors affect the rate
 Define "F", and "F0" values and their application
 Determine the process time
 Describe the purpose of exhausting and closing.
 Describe the three major heating sources of in-container sterilization; their special feature and examples
 Describe the features in ultrahigh-temperature process, direct and indirect systems
 Provide examples and products character for indirect systems including plate heat exchanger, tubular heat
exchangers, scraped-surface heat exchanger and Jupiter double-cone heat exchanger
 Describe how they affect the quality of foods

3. Dehydration
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Describe dehydration, its purpose and benefits
 Understand the mechanism of drying and describe the modes of water migration from the inside to the surface,
and from the surface to the surroundings
 Describe the drying curve in terms of moisture' content vs drying time as well as the drying rate vs the moisture
content.
 Describe the three characteristics of air to increase the drying rate.
 Differentiate between hot-air driers and heated surface driers, provide examples for each class
 Describe the features in different types of driers.
 Describe the purpose of the agglomerated powder
 Describe how dehydrate would affect the quality of foods

4. Pasteurization
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Describe pasteurization and its purpose
 Tell how pasteurization works
 Describe how the D-value determines the extent of pasteurization
 Name the two major groups of equipment for pasteurization of liquid food
 Describe the features in different pasteurizers.
 Describe how pasteurization would affect the quality of foods

Part IV Low temperature processing
1. Chilling
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand the purpose, principles and characteristics of chilling in extending the shelf-life of foods
 Distinguish the factors that determined the shelf life of fresh and processed chilled foods
 Understand cook-chill systems as a combination of high and low temperature processing to extend the shelf-life
of cooked foods
 Classify the different mechanical chilling equipments based on the chilling medium
 Compare the different characteristics of some common refrigerants
 Understand cryogenic chilling as an alternative low temperature processing and compare the characteristics of
some common cryogens
 Describe the applications of cryogenic cooling in foods
 Discuss the possible effect of chilling on foods including the sensory, microbiological and physiological aspects
of foods

2. Freezing and frozen-food storage
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand the recent frozen food market
 Describe the underlying principles of freezing in food preservation
 Understand the physical changes that happen in food during the process of freezing including ice crystal
formation, solute concentration, and volume change
 Understand the factors that determine the freezing time
 Differentiate mechanical freezer equipments based on their designs in freezing medium and mode of operations
 Understand the applications of different mechanical freezing equipments to different food categories
 Discuss the advantages of cryogenic freezers over mechanical ones
 Understand the principles and food applications of cryogenic freezers
 Discuss the possible changes happened during frozen-food storage
 Compare the effect on food quality produced by slow freezing and quick freezing in terms of ice crystal formation
 Describe the effect of temperature fluctuations during frozen storage in term of recrystallization and freezer burn
 Understand the monitoring of temperature fluctuations in frozen foods
 Understand the evaluation of shelf-life of frozen foods
 Understand thawing is not an exact reverse process of freezing
 Describe the equipment and considerations for thawing

courses.description: Community nutrition recognizes that the control and prevention of nutrition problems are not merely biomedical in nature, but are embedded in the community of the affected individuals. A community nutritionist assesses and monitors not only physiological and dietary, but also social, cultural, technological and psychological information from many sources to determine needs and identify opportunities for sound, appropriate interventions that improve nutritional health. Because well-conceived nutrition surveys are basic tools for prioritising problems and deciding program plans and evaluations to provide better nutrition services to the public, the course will first introduce community nutrition survey design to the students. Making healthier choices, however, requires lifelong change in thinking and action at both individual and community levels. The rest of the course examines applications of current individual and group nutritional behaviour change theories to promote healthier diets.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Discuss the work of community nutrition in preventing disease and promoting health

- Design a nutrition survey, demonstrating appropriate use of methodology and statistics

- Discover findings, and arragne, interpret and present results from a nutrition survey

- Appreciate the interrelationships of social, cultural, technological and psychological factors in determining food choice and eating habits

- Describe how to apply some theoretical models of individual, interpersonal, and group health behaviors to designing nutrition intervention strategies

courses.description: Medical nutrition therapy examines the theory and practice behind the prevention and treatment of diseases with the help of diet. This course will introduce the etiology and dietary management of selected diet-related diseases including obesity; anorexia and other eating disorders; diabetes mellitus; cardiovascular diseases including hyperlipidemias; diseases of the alimentary canal, liver, kidney and gall bladder; pancreatitis; food allergy and cancer. It will also cover nutritional management for AIDS patients, interaction of drugs and nutrients, and aspects of dietary therapy in Chinese Medicine. The related applied aspects of dietetics, including the practical skills associated with the preparation, use and evaluation of special diets, and the development of interview and communication skills, will also be covered.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to be able to:
1. assess the nutritional status using simple nutritional assessment methods
2. distinguish between enteral nutrition and parenteral nutrition as nutritional support for patients with special needs
3. recognize the interactions between drugs and nutrients and how these interactions affect nutrition therapy
4. describe the etiology, treatment and dietary management of selected diet-related diseases including obesity and
diabetes mellitus; diseases of the heart, blood vessels, and lungs; gastrointestinal diseases, renal diseases,
food allergy and food intolerance, cancer and AIDS
5. discuss the role of Chinese Medicine as an alternate means of dietary therapy for some common diseases

courses.description: This course explores various stages of food product development, and the importance of quality assurance. Topics include idea development, taste-panelling, shelflife, local food regulations, the ISO standards, GMP, HACCP, quality control tools, statistic quality control and product evaluation.
courses.learning_outcomes:
FNSC4170 contains twelve parts:
Part I: Introduction and definition
Part II: Idea generation
Part III: Idea screening
Part IV: Sensory evaluation
Part V: Shelflife of foods
Part VI: Food laws
Part VII: HACCP
Part VIII: GMP
Part IX: ISO standards
Part X: Quality control tools
Part XI: Statistic quality control
Part XII: Product evaluation

The learning outcomes:
Part I Introduction and definition
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Define new food products
 Classify different new products with real-world examples
 Define and differentiate line extension, reposition, new forms, reformulation, new packaging, innovative products
and creative products
 Understand the driving forces of new product development
 Describe product life cycle
 Describe why company needs new products
 Describe different phases in new product development

Part II Idea generation
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Identify the various sources of product development ideas
 Differentiate the internal and external sources of new ideas
 Obtain ideas in conferences, exhibits, trade shows, public libraries, etc.
 Generate information from the total market place analysis
 Describe the purpose of analysis of purchases
 Master the gap analysis to generate product ideas

Part III Idea screening
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Explain the purpose of idea screening and the elements involved in the process
 Explain the purpose and the skill of new product development team
 Identify the function of each team member

Part IV Sensory evaluation
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Define “Sensory Evaluation” as specify by the Institute of Food Technologists (IFT)
 Describe the general conditions of the subjects carrying out sensory evaluation
 Describe the various sensory techniques used as described by the IFT
 Describe the setup and environment of a sensory facility
 Understand the operation of the “Different tests” including pair comparison, due trio, triangle, ranking, rating
difference tests
 Define and determine the threshold value
 Describe the elements in Flavor Profile, Quantitative Descriptive Analysis
 Describe the purpose and the considerations in the application of the “Affective Test”
 Describe the consideration when designing questionnaires for sensory evaluation

Part V: Shelflife of foods
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Describe the importance of shelflife to food
 Identify the various intrinsic and extrinsic factors affecting the shelflife of food
 Understand the mechanisms involved in the deterioration of food
 Differentiate between the direct and indirect approach to shelflife determination
 Describe the various elements in the stages of shelflife determination
 Make use of the Arrhenius equation in the determination of shelflife and understand the limitations of the indirect
shelflife determination approach

Part VI: Food laws
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Describe where to search the food laws in Hong Kong
 Identify the major areas of food laws covered in Hong Kong
 Define what a food and an additive
 Identify the sweeteners used in Hong Kong Food Law
 Describe the major contents of the harmful substances regulated in the local food law
 Identify the prohibited substances in Hong Kong
 Describe the major categories of additive described in the local Food Law
 Define mineral oil and describe its conditional usage
 Describe the major categories of coloring matter used locally
 Differentiate the difference between preservatives and antioxidants used in food
 Identify the metal contaminants permitted in Hong Kong
 Describe the major content in the composition and labeling law

Part VII: HACCP
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Define the essence in HACCP
 Identify the 7 principles
 Recognize the various physical, chemical and biological hazards
 Able to use the decision trees to identify critical point for raw materials and actual operation
 Describe the 4 stages in a HACCP system
 Describe the steps in HACCP plan and provide example for each step
 Understand how long and what types of the HACCP records should be kept

Part VIII: GMP
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Define quality and explain why it is important
 Understand the implications of the customer surveys towards unsatisfied customers
 Describe the evolution of quality assurance philosophy
 Define the purpose of “Good Manufacturing Practice” (GMP)

Part IX: ISO Standards
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Define the mission of ISO
 Understand the background for ISO Standards
 Describe the core standards
 Understand the steps in certification process
 Differentiate between accreditation and certification
 Tell the limitation of the certification

Part X: Quality control tools
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Differentiate the various problem solving tools
 Describe the basic rules and steps in brainstorming
 Describe the function of pareto analysis and its steps
 Describe how to construct a process flow diagram
 Utilize the cause and effect diagram
 Understand when to use the control chart

Part XI: Statistic quality control
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Understand the terms used and recognize the pattern in the control chart
 Understand the different types of control charts and their application
 Differentiate different types of quality defects
 Describe the difference between sampling inspection and control chart
 Describe different sampling types
 Understand how to use sampling table such as JIS Z 9002 and MIL-STD-105D

Part XII: Product evaluation
Objectives: After these lectures, a student should be able to
 Decide what kind of method to use to measure the concentration of sugar and salt
 The function of a refractometer and its principle
 Describe the quality of brine
 Describe the method and the principle to measure sugar and sucrose content in potato
 Describe the direct and indirect tests to measure the undesirable odors presence with the packaging materials
 Describe the latest technology in measuring odor and taste, its working principle and limitations
 Describe ways to measure food color and texture
 Describe methods to determine the maturity in food
 Describe the measurements to reflect the quality condition in fat and oil
 Decide the method to measure total acidity and pH
 Evaluate the integrity of package and container

This course is specifically designed for final-year Nutritionist Stream students in FNS Programme. Students should have completed FNSC4906 Internship prior to taking this course. Students are expected to apply scientific evidence-based nutrition knowledge and to carry out the task with the demonstration of professional behavior and the compliance in the code of ethics and standards of professional conduct. courses.description: This course explores the origins and etiology, dietary therapies and population-based strategies to overcome the nutrition-related chronic disease burden globally, regionally and in Hong Kong. Multidisciplinary researchers and practitioners will discuss how modern culture, including food consumption and lifestyles, produces this noncommunicable disease burden, leaving governments challenged to fnd effective policy solutions.

For students in MPhil-PhD Food and Nutritional Sciences or MSc Nutrition, Food Science and Technology
Not for students who have taken LSCI5812
courses.learning_outcomes:
After this course, the students will be able to
- understand how nutrition transition will affect our diet by referring to historical, cultural, biological, and economical aspects
- describe how modern diets and lifestyle give rise to the global and local epidemic and individual/societal burdens of non-communicable diseases (NCD)
- recognize the influence of NCD on individual’s nutritional status and describe role of medical nutrition therapy (MNT) in the management and treatment of NCD such as cancer, diabetes and metabolic syndrome, obesity, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, and renal disease etc.
- describe the role of nutrition in health care, the nutrition care process and methods of nutrition assessment, specialized nutrition support and geriatric nutrition

courses.description: Food can be contaminated at any stage of its production and handling with naturally occurring toxicants and/or man-made chemicals that have adverse health effects to humans. The objective of this course is to gain knowledge on the key concepts and principles of food safety and toxicology. Students are expected to develop an understanding of the nature and properties of the toxic substances in foods as well as the nature and magnitude of the hazard they represent to humans, with the aim of preventing health risks due to food intake. Topics on food safety include food hygiene, food poisoning, food legislation and food safety control systems. Topics on food toxicology include its general principles, biochemical and physiological mechanisms of action of food toxicants, and methods for food safety assessment. Emphasis will be placed on the evaluation of current issues in food safety toxicology including risk assessment and management.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in MSc Nutrition, Food Science and Technology or MPhil-PhD Food and Nutritional Sciences or BSc Food and Nutritional Sciences
Not for students who have taken LSCI5843
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to be able to:
1. gain knowledge on the key concepts and principles of food safety and toxicology
2. understand the nature and properties of the toxic substances in foods as well as the nature and magnitude of the hazard they represent to humans,
3. understand the general principles, biochemical and physiological mechanisms of action of food toxicants, and methods for food safety assessment
4. understand the basic principles of food hygiene and food poisoning to prevent health risks due to food intake.
5. understand food legislation and food safety control systems, as well as risk analysis
